newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung backs away from auto report after criticism.
newsitem.headline: Samsung backs away from auto report after criticism.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Motors Inc bowed to strong criticism from its competitors on Monday and backed away from a dispute over the need to restructure the country's struggling car industry.

"We are not interested in any merger and acquisition deals and have no plan to seek them," said Samsung Motors spokesman Han Jae-yoon. "We are already busy enough in proceeding with our scheduled projects."

Samsung's oblique statement followed a storm of controversy over a leaked internal report suggesting that restructuring was needed to avert a possible crisis in the car industry stemming from over-investment and unstable demand and supply.

The Samsung report was interpreted as an attempt by the upstart car maker to win support for a possible hostile takeover of an existing manufacturer. Kia Motors Corp was considered the mostly likely target.
But the report, widely publicised last week, brought strong condemnation from existing industry players.
Kia last week threatened to sue Samsung for asserting in the report that Kia was experiencing "managerial conflicts".
Earlier on Monday, Hyundai Motor Co and five other South Korean auto makers vowed to take joint action against Samsung.

"We are still thinking about what measures we will take. But Samsung must publicly apologise for disseminating false rumours," said Chung Mong-kyu, chairman of the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
Chung, also chairman of South Korea's largest car maker, Hyundai Motor, said Samsung was not qualified to discuss the restructuring issue because Samsung could be the cause of over-capacity.
The six companies said the Samsung Group should be first to leave the industry if restructuring became inevitable.

The statement was jointly issued by chief executives of the manufacturers' association, Hyundai Motor, Kia Motors Corp, Daewoo Motor Co, Asia Motors Co, Ssangyong Motor Co and Hyundai Precision and Industry Co.

The statement also asked the government to closely watch the progress of Samsung's car making project to ensure that Samsung kept the promises it put forward in 1994 when the government approved its licence to import auto-manufacturing technology.
At that time, Samsung pledged not to disrupt existing makers' parts supply networks and not to recruit their workers.
Samsung has said the report did not represent the company's official position.
"We don't see the need to respond to an episode that flared over a private document," said a Samsung statement issued to clarify its position after the meeting of six companies.
But analysts said Samsung, despite its denials, probably was interested in a takeover deal as a short cut to success.
"We cannot possibly think of Samsung succeeding in the car industry without it taking over any existing company," said Ji Sung-chul, an analyst at LG Economic Research Institute.

Analysts said Samsung might be troubled to meet its schedule of turning out 500,000 cars annually by 2002 because of high construction costs and difficulties obtaining technology from its Japanese partner Nissan Motor Co.

"Nissan is now much healthier financially than three years ago when Samsung signed a technical aid contract with it. The Japanese firm is less interested in helping Samsung," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
Others said restructuring might be a good idea.

"The six companies' statement seems to be aimed at protecting their vested interest. The issue of restructuring should be discussed for the interest of consumers and the national economy, not for producers' interest," said Yang Dong-ki, an analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
